title: image scp: add --compression-format and --compression-level
body:
`podman save` writes docker-archive layers uncompressed, so `podman image scp` puts the whole archive on the wire as is. Today people work around that with `podman save | zstd`, a manual copy and `podman load` on the far side.

This adds `--compression-format` (gzip, zstd) and `--compression-level` so the transfer does it itself. Nothing is needed on the destination: `podman load` detects the compression from the stream and decompresses it.

Compression happens on whichever host produces the archive, so only compressed bytes cross the network:

- **Local source** — the archive is compressed on the fly into the ssh stream feeding the remote `podman image load`, via the c/image compression package. No second temporary file, nothing buffered in full.
- **Remote source** — the archive has to be compressed there, and the only thing we can do on that host is run a command, so the matching compressor is invoked over ssh between the save and the copy. That is also why the format list is limited to algorithms available as a command of the same name.
- **Two users on the same machine** — nothing crosses a network, so a requested format is reported as ignored rather than refused.

Measured on `quay.io/libpod/alpine`, docker-archive goes from 5.85 MB to 2.72 MB with zstd. An oci-archive keeps whatever compression its layers already have, so there the gain is negligible (~98%); the man page records the difference.

Fixes: #23192

```release-note
podman image scp now supports --compression-format and --compression-level to compress the transferred image archive.
```

comments.body: Can you add a release note along the lines of “podman image scp now supports --compression-format and --compression-level”

Changes LGTM overall, but definitely want other eyeballs on this one.
THanks @scallaway

> Can you add a release note along the lines of “podman image scp now supports --compression-format and --compression-level”

Done!

> Just a drive-by — but, really, do we _want_ to commit to this?!
> 
> I’d think that `image scp` should, ideally, be magic and do “the right thing”. Why would users _want_ to worry about compression formats, and compatibility, and having command-line compression implementations installed? (And do we want to worry about the very inaccurate handling of spaces in remote ssh?)

I am open to suggestions, I was just trying to unravel a knot that we're currently running into at our company.

We have both images that use `gzip` _and_ `zstd` and currently we're having to convert everything to `gzip` so we can use `podman save`. Ideally we'd keep the formatting dependent on the team managing the image and the command doesn't care.

Whether we make it explicit where the user declares the compression, or Podman does this automagically is certainly a decision to be made. I'm willing to defer that to you as maintainers rather than me as a first-time contributor!

> We have both images that use gzip and zstd and currently we're having to convert everything to gzip so we can use podman save. Ideally we'd keep the formatting dependent on the team managing the image and the command doesn't care.

Wait, are you saying that Zstd-compressed images on the registry, after pulling, can’t be stored using `podman save`, because that outright fails? That would be rather surprising, and something that should be fixed directly.
